questions.question: Define rejuvenation and explain its two main families of causes, naming the technical term for each.
questions.expected_answer: Rejuvenation is the process by which a graded river regains erosive energy and resumes vigorous vertical downcutting, because the relationship between the river and its base level has changed. Family one: a fall in base level — eustatic change — when world sea level drops, for example during a glacial period when water is locked into ice sheets, stranding the mouth above the new sea level and steepening the lower profile. Family two: uplift of the land — tectonic or isostatic change — when the crust rises beneath the river, as the southern African interior has done, steepening every gradient. Both raise velocity and energy; the knickpoint where new profile meets old migrates upstream. A local third trigger is increased discharge, for instance after river capture.

questions.question: Name and briefly explain the four landform signatures of rejuvenation.
questions.expected_answer: The knickpoint: a sharp break of slope in the long profile, usually a waterfall or rapids — like Howick Falls on the uMngeni — retreating upstream as the river cuts its lip. Paired terraces: remnants of the old floodplain stranded as flat benches at matching heights on both sides after the river trenched its own valley floor; repeated rejuvenation builds a staircase, oldest at the top. Valley-in-a-valley: the cross-sectional form of a fresh, steep V incised into the floor of the old broad valley, with the terraces as the old floor's edges. Incised meanders: pre-existing loops cut vertically into rock as winding gorges — entrenched meanders symmetric from fast vertical cutting, ingrown meanders asymmetric where slower incision allowed continued sideways shift.

questions.question: Describe the mechanism of river capture and label the five features of the capture diagram, adding one after-effect for each river.
questions.expected_answer: A stronger river — with a steeper gradient, softer rock or more rainfall — extends its source backwards by headward erosion through the watershed until its headwaters intersect the weaker river's channel; offered a lower, steeper exit, the weak river's upper course diverts into the strong one. Labels: the captor stream (the thief, now enlarged), the captured stream (the redirected upper course), the elbow of capture (the sharp unnatural bend at the diversion), the misfit stream (the beheaded lower course, undersized for its broad valley), and the wind gap (the abandoned dry valley through the high ground). After-effects: the captor's increased discharge gives it new energy and it often rejuvenates, while the starved misfit's valley silts up and may become swampy.
